# 1. What the Research Found

**MONITORING. Re-check window: the OECD Environmental Finance publication series' own article-level pages, and the ITF-OECD SIPA methodology document, at the next monitoring pass.**

The captured pool for this item contains one substantive source: a peer-reviewed *Scientific Reports* article by Habib, Abd Rahman, Hashmi, and Ali on green finance and environmental decentralization in OECD countries. The other five captured URLs under the OECD domain returned only site-navigation structure (topic menus, country-list footers), and the ITF-OECD decarbonisation methodology PDF returned a Cloudflare security-verification interstitial; none of the six grounds any claim below (see Section 6).

FACT: "Article Open access Published: 01 August 2025" *Source: Habib et al., "Green finance and environmental decentralization drive OECD low carbon transitions," Scientific Reports. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-11967-y

FACT: "The study employs 'a panel dataset comprising 44 OECD countries, spanning 1995–2022.'" *Source: Habib et al., Scientific Reports. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-11967-y

FACT: "Ecological footprint serves as an indicator of sustainable development." *Source: Habib et al., Scientific Reports. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-11967-y

FACT: "The study describes green finance as 'financial and investment activities geared towards achieving environmental benefits', with measures including 'Financial investment directed towards climate change mitigation and climate change adaptation technologies...'" *Source: Habib et al., Scientific Reports. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-11967-y

FACT: "our findings demonstrate that green finance significantly enhances sustainable development across countries." *Source: Habib et al., Scientific Reports. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-11967-y

FACT: "More specifically: 'green finance and environmental decentralization exhibit a positive, statistically significant influence on sustainable development in OECD countries...'" *Source: Habib et al., Scientific Reports. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-11967-y

FACT: "The study applies 'Using OLS, Oster coefficient stability, Lewbel 2SLS, and Kiviet instrumental variable techniques.'" *Source: Habib et al., Scientific Reports. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-11967-y

FACT: "A new index was devised that incorporates multiple indicators of environmental decentralization." *Source: Habib et al., Scientific Reports. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-11967-y

*Analytical inference:* the study's methods (OLS with Oster coefficient stability, Lewbel 2SLS, and Kiviet instrumental-variable techniques) are the standard econometric toolkit for addressing endogeneity in a country-panel design; this is a methodology strength note, not itself a finding the workspace can cite operationally.

# 2. Why This Finding Matters Operationally and Commercially

FACT: "it is imperative that OECD countries formulate and implement policies that foster green financing and empower local governments." *Source: Habib et al., Scientific Reports. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-11967-y

*Operational implication:* the authors' own policy conclusion, that OECD governments should formulate policies fostering green financing and empowering local governments to reduce pollution through climate-mitigation and -adaptation technology innovation, is the same policy direction that already generates the regulatory instruments a freight-forwarding workspace answers to on OECD trade lanes (SAF blending mandates, emissions trading systems, green public-procurement criteria). This study is evidence the underlying finance-and-policy environment is statistically active, not merely declared.

FACT: "the OECD's parallel work areas: 'Finance and investment for climate goals' and 'Finance and investment for environmental goals'" *Source: Habib et al., Scientific Reports (citing the OECD's own published work areas). https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-11967-y

*Analytical inference:* these are the same OECD work areas that feed the finance-and-investment policy instruments referenced above; the study's finding of a statistically significant green-finance effect corroborates that OECD-jurisdiction finance and disclosure pressure is a durable trend rather than a one-off initiative.

FACT: "this study incorporated crucial control variables such as economic abundance, energy transition, financial development..." *Source: Habib et al., Scientific Reports. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-11967-y

*Operational implication:* because the study's own design controls for financial development and urbanisation at the country level, it supports comparisons ACROSS OECD countries in general terms; it does not supply a mode-specific or forwarder-specific cost or emissions figure the workspace can quote to a client.

# 3. What the Finding Changes for Strategy, Claims, or Decisions

**1. Client sustainability dialogue -- directional grounding, not a performance number.**

*Analytical inference:* the study provides peer-reviewed support for the proposition that green-finance mechanisms in OECD countries are producing a measurable, statistically significant effect. The workspace can reference this in client conversations as evidence that the macro-level policy and finance environment supports continued regulatory tightening, without overclaiming a specific cost or emissions trajectory this study does not supply.

**2. Procurement and tender positioning.**

*Analytical inference:* clients in OECD jurisdictions operating under CSRD, ISSB, or an equivalent disclosure framework increasingly ask suppliers, including freight forwarders, for Scope 3 data and sustainability credentials. The study's confirmation of a green-finance effect strengthens the case for the workspace to prioritise its own emissions-data infrastructure, on the basis that the policy environment driving those client requests is statistically durable.

**3. No specific cost or rate decision is changed by this study alone.**

*Analytical inference:* the study operates at the macroeconomic country-panel level. It supplies no mode-specific cost projection, no carrier-level data, and no freight-specific investment figure. A decision on a specific fuel-surcharge structure, SAF purchase agreement, or carbon-credit strategy still requires carrier-specific and route-specific data this study does not provide.

# 4. Client Conversation Talking Points and Public Position

**What the workspace can credibly say:**

- "Peer-reviewed research covering 44 OECD countries from 1995 to 2022 finds that green finance, investment directed at climate mitigation and adaptation, has a statistically significant positive association with sustainable development outcomes across those countries." This is directly supportable from the study's own stated finding.
- "The policy direction the researchers recommend, more green-financing policy and empowered local government action, is consistent with the SAF mandates, ETS expansions, and green-procurement criteria our compliance function already tracks in OECD jurisdictions."

**Pitfalls to avoid:**

- Do not cite this study for a specific cost figure, an emissions-reduction percentage, or a carrier-level performance claim. It is a country-panel study; it has no forwarder-level output.
- *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a specific air, ocean, or road freight activity of the workspace's own qualifies as "green finance" under a taxonomy such as the EU Taxonomy or the ICMA Green Bond Principles is a legal and regulatory question this academic study does not answer.
- Do not cite the OECD Environmental Finance publication series, or the linked "Finance and investment for climate/environmental goals" topic pages, for a specific data point: every one of those captured pages returned navigation structure only, not article content (Section 6).
- Do not cite the ITF-OECD SIPA decarbonisation methodology document in a client conversation: the capture attempt returned a Cloudflare verification page, not the document's content (Section 6).

# 5. What the Finding Does Not Resolve

GAP: Specific figures, thematic focus areas, and policy recommendations from the OECD Environmental Finance publication series itself are not available from primary sources as of the export date; the five captured OECD URLs (Environmental Finance landing page in both the bare and www forms, the Finance and Investment for Environmental Goals topic page, the Green Finance and Investment publication page, and the OECD's climate-finance-mobilisation tracking page) each returned only the OECD site's own topic-menu and country-list navigation chrome, not article body text.

GAP: The ITF-OECD SIPA decarbonisation methodology document's content, including any transport-sector-specific decarbonisation pathway analysis it may contain, is not available from primary sources as of the export date; the capture returned a Cloudflare security-verification interstitial rather than the PDF's content.

GAP: The study does not disaggregate its ecological-footprint outcome by economic sector, so whether the country-level improvement it measures is driven primarily by the transport sector, as opposed to energy or another sector, is not established by this source.

FACT: "Article Open access Published: 01 August 2025" *Source: Habib et al., Scientific Reports. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-11967-y

*Operational implication:* the workspace's next monitoring pass should attempt a fresh retrieval of the OECD Environmental Finance series' individual publication pages (the ISSN 1990-1135 series) and the ITF-OECD SIPA methodology PDF, since neither yielded content on this pass, and both may bear directly on the workspace's modal decarbonisation planning.

- 1 August 2025: the Habib et al. study was published open access in Scientific Reports; this is the finding's own dated anchor, in the absence of any regulatory or programme date in the captured pool.

# 1. What the Research Found

**MONITORING. Re-check window: the next regular monitoring pass, for a published (non-preprint) journal version and any commercial routing-product adoption.**

FACT: "Authors: Poulad Moradi , Joachim Arts , Josué C. Velázquez-Martínez" *Source: arXiv:2306.01687. https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01687

FACT: "Title: Load Asymptotics and Dynamic Speed Optimization for the Greenest Path Problem: A Comprehensive Analysis" *Source: arXiv:2306.01687. https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01687

FACT: "We study the effect of using high-resolution elevation data on the selection of the most fuel-efficient(greenest) path for different trucks in various urban road networks." *Source: arXiv:2306.01687 abstract. https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01687

FACT: "The researchers adapt a variant of the Comprehensive Modal Emission Model(CMEM) to show that the optimal speed and the greenest path are slope dependent (dynamic)." *Source: arXiv:2306.01687 abstract. https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01687

FACT: "When there are no elevation changes in a road network, the most fuel-efficient path is the shortest path with a constant (static) optimal speed." *Source: arXiv:2306.01687 abstract. https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01687

FACT: "However, if the network is not flat, then the shortest path is not necessarily the greenest path, and the optimal driving speed is dynamic." *Source: arXiv:2306.01687 abstract. https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01687

FACT: "The paper's authors prove that the greenest path converges to an asymptotic greenest path as the payload approaches infinity and that this limiting path is attained for a finite load." *Source: arXiv:2306.01687 abstract. https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01687

FACT: "Using extensive numerical experiments, we benchmark the CO2emissions reduction of our dynamic speed and the greenest path policies against policies that ignore elevation changes." *Source: arXiv:2306.01687 abstract. https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01687

FACT: "Numerical experiments across 25 major cities on 6 continents showcase the CO2 reduction prowess of our dynamic speed and greenest path policies." *Source: MIT Sustainable Supply Chain Lab, "Sustainable Transportation" page (co-authored by researchers at MIT CTL and the University of Luxembourg Centre for Logistics and Supply Chain Management). https://sustainable.mit.edu/sustainable-transportation

FACT: "the main determinants of the CO2emissions reduction potential are the variation of the road gradients along the shortest path as well as the relative elevation of the source from the destination." *Source: arXiv:2306.01687 abstract. https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01687

# 2. Why This Finding Matters Operationally and Commercially

FACT: "Using Speed data estimates for rush hour in New York City, we test CO2emissions reduction by comparing the greenest paths with optimized speeds against the fastest paths with traffic congestion." *Source: arXiv:2306.01687 abstract. https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01687

*Operational implication:* the study's own New York City test case, comparing the elevation-aware greenest path against the fastest path, is the closest the pool comes to an operational case study; it is still a modelled benchmark against traffic congestion data, not a field trial with a carrier's actual telematics.

FACT: "The authors observe numerically that the greenest path quickly diverges from the shortest path and attains the asymptotic greenest path even for moderate payloads." *Source: MIT Sustainable Supply Chain Lab, "Sustainable Transportation" page. https://sustainable.mit.edu/sustainable-transportation

*Analytical inference:* because the greenest path diverges from the shortest path "even for moderate payloads" per the study's own finding, the fuel-saving effect this research identifies is not limited to the heaviest loads on a fleet's roster; it is potentially relevant across a road-freight operator's typical payload range, subject to the limitations noted in Section 5.

FACT: "The authors report that while speed optimization on uphill arcs can significantly help CO2reduction,the potential to leverage gravity for acceleration on downhill arcs is limited due to traffic congestion." *Source: arXiv:2306.01687 abstract. https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01687

*Operational implication:* this asymmetry (uphill speed optimisation helps; downhill gravity-assisted savings are congestion-limited) means the fuel-efficiency gain the study identifies is route-topology- and traffic-condition-specific, not a flat percentage a workspace can apply uniformly to a road lane.

# 3. What the Finding Changes for Strategy, Claims, or Decisions

**1. Route-planning technology evaluation, not carrier rate renegotiation.**

*Analytical inference:* if the workspace evaluates or specifies a routing/telematics vendor for road-freight subcontractors, this study is evidence that elevation-aware dynamic-speed routing is an active, credentialed (MIT CTL co-authored) research area with a documented CO2-reduction mechanism -- a reasonable question to put to a routing-technology vendor is whether its algorithm accounts for road-gradient variation, not merely distance.

**2. Do not renegotiate carrier rates on this study's basis.**

*Analytical inference:* the reduction potential this study reports is modelled and benchmarked against comparison policies in a numerical experiment; it is not a field-measured fuel saving attributable to any specific carrier's actual operations. Citing it as the basis for a rate concession would overstate what the study establishes.

# 4. Client Conversation Talking Points and Public Position

**What the workspace can credibly say:**

- "Current MIT-affiliated research (with the University of Luxembourg) shows that elevation-aware dynamic-speed routing algorithms can reduce CO2 emissions on road freight lanes beyond what standard shortest-path routing achieves, with the effect demonstrated across a numerical study spanning 25 major cities on 6 continents."
- "The research finds this effect holds even for moderate payloads, not only the heaviest loads, though the actual saving depends on a lane's own road-gradient profile."

**Pitfalls to avoid:**

- *Analytical inference:* do not cite a specific percentage CO2-reduction figure as applicable to the workspace's own road operations -- the study benchmarks a modelled algorithm against comparison routing policies in a numerical experiment, not against any carrier's measured, real-world fuel consumption.
- Do not present this as a commercially available routing product the workspace can specify today; the captured pool does not identify one built on this specific methodology (Section 5).

# 5. What the Finding Does Not Resolve

GAP: The study is a modelled, algorithmic result. It does not address whether drivers follow algorithmically derived routes in practice, or what real-world compliance rate an elevation-aware routing recommendation would achieve on an actual road-freight lane.

GAP: The finding does not support renegotiating carrier rates based on a claimed fuel saving, because the reduction potential is modelled and benchmarked in a numerical experiment, not measured against any specific carrier's real-world operations.

GAP: The source blocks do not identify a commercially available routing product built on this specific methodology.

GAP: The finding does not address how road-leg routing optimisation interacts with air or ocean schedule constraints at intermodal handoff points, which is the actual planning question for a multimodal freight-forwarding workspace.

FACT: "Related DOI : https://doi.org/10.1007/s00291-024-00793-9" *Source: arXiv:2306.01687. https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01687

*Operational implication:* the related DOI indicates the paper has a formal journal-published counterpart; the workspace's next monitoring pass should attempt to retrieve that journal version directly, since a peer-reviewed published version may include material (a published commercial application, a broader empirical validation) the preprint abstract captured here does not.

FACT: "[Submitted on 2 Jun 2023 ( v1 ), last revised 30 May 2025 (this version, v2)]" *Source: arXiv:2306.01687 submission history. https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01687

- 2 Jun 2023: the study was first submitted to arXiv as v1.
- 30 May 2025: the study was last revised (v2), the version captured for this brief.

# 6. Sources

|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Moradi, Arts and Velazquez-Martinez, "Load Asymptotics and Dynamic Speed Optimization for the Greenest Path Problem: A Comprehensive Analysis," arXiv:2306.01687 | Academic preprint (math.OC / econ.EM) | https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01687 |
| 2 | MIT Sustainable Supply Chain Lab, "Sustainable Transportation" | Academic research centre (MIT CTL) | https://sustainable.mit.edu/sustainable-transportation |

*Note:* two captured blocks ground no claim in this brief: the MIT CTL publication page for this paper
(ctl.mit.edu) returned a "Page not found" error, and the University of Luxembourg's City Logistics
Freight Lab page (uni.lu) returned a 403 "request blocked" error page.

This item profiles the Carbon Trust, a UK-incorporated certification and advisory organisation, drawing on its Companies House filing, its own Route to Net Zero Standard and Maritime Decarbonisation pages, and its Wikipedia entry.

FACT: "No shareholders. We are financially independent and invest our profit back into enhancing the breadth and reach of our work." *Source: Carbon Trust Impact Report 2024 (via publications.carbontrust.com). https://publications.carbontrust.com/

FACT: "8 Offices 75 Countries reached through our work" *Source: Carbon Trust Impact Report 2024. https://publications.carbontrust.com/

FACT: "282+ Experts who advise on Net Zero transition plans, science-based targets, energy transition, sustainable finance, policy, climate disclosures and communication." *Source: Carbon Trust Impact Report 2024. https://publications.carbontrust.com/

FACT: "2,796+ Organisations supported to date." *Source: Carbon Trust Impact Report 2024. https://publications.carbontrust.com/

FACT: "Impact report 2024 OUR MISSION To accelerate the move to a decarbonised future" *Source: Carbon Trust Impact Report 2024. https://publications.carbontrust.com/

FACT: "This article needs additional citations for verification . Please help improve this article by adding citations to reliable sources . Unsourced material may be challenged and removed." *Source: "Carbon Trust," Wikipedia. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_Trust

*Analytical inference:* the Wikipedia entry's own citations-needed banner is a signal to weight that source as secondary/encyclopaedic background only, never as the basis for a specific figure cited to a client; every figure quoted in this brief is instead drawn from the Carbon Trust's own primary pages or its Companies House filing.

# 2. Why This Finding Matters Operationally and Commercially

FACT: "The Carbon Trust Route to Net Zero Standard is the only certification that guides and supports your organisation on your journey towards Net Zero and climate leadership." *Source: Route to Net Zero Standard, The Carbon Trust. https://www.carbontrust.com/what-we-do/net-zero-transition-planning-and-delivery/route-to-net-zero-standard

FACT: "we will independently verify your carbon reductions, and guide you in taking the next steps towards decarbonisation." *Source: Route to Net Zero Standard, The Carbon Trust. https://www.carbontrust.com/what-we-do/net-zero-transition-planning-and-delivery/route-to-net-zero-standard

*Operational implication:* for a workspace that is itself asked by a client or tender to demonstrate a credentialed Net Zero pathway, the Route to Net Zero Standard and its independent-verification structure is a specific, named certification option; the operational question is whether it, or a scheme like it, is the one the workspace's own client procurement frameworks already recognise (Section 5).

FACT: "It is the world's first independent certification for organisations that are measuring, managing and reducing greenhouse gas (CO2e) emissio" *Source: "Carbon Trust," Wikipedia, describing the separate Carbon Trust Standard for Supply Chain. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_Trust

*Analytical inference:* this is a distinct certification (the Supply Chain Standard) from the Route to Net Zero Standard quoted above; the two should not be conflated when the workspace names a specific Carbon Trust certification to a client.

FACT: "the Carbon Trust has not received UKAS accreditation." *Source: "Carbon Trust," Wikipedia. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_Trust

*Analytical inference:* the Carbon Trust's certification schemes are not themselves UKAS-accredited per the Wikipedia entry's own note; a workspace evaluating a Carbon Trust certification against a client's own accreditation requirements should confirm what accreditation standard that specific client requires before assuming equivalence.

FACT: "represents almost 3% of global CO2 emissions" *Source: Maritime Decarbonisation, The Carbon Trust, footnoted to "Fourth Greenhouse Gas Study 2020 (imo.org)". https://www.carbontrust.com/what-we-do/market-transformation/maritime-decarbonisation

FACT: "We are a founding partner of Blue Visby, which exists to make shipping more sustainable by eradicating certain maritime practices to reduce a ship's carbon footprint." *Source: Maritime Decarbonisation, The Carbon Trust. https://www.carbontrust.com/what-we-do/market-transformation/maritime-decarbonisation

*Operational implication:* for a workspace with ocean freight exposure, the Carbon Trust's own citation of the IMO's near-3%-of-global-emissions figure for shipping, plus its founding role in the Blue Visby scheme (aimed at reducing unnecessary fuel consumption through operational changes rather than new vessel technology), is directly relevant background for client conversations about ocean-leg emissions reduction levers that do not require fleet replacement.

FACT: "our in-depth Commercial Readiness of Alternative Shipping Fuels Study assessed the merits and drawbacks of five alternative shipping fuels across each supply chain stage, with a focus on the European context." *Source: Maritime Decarbonisation, The Carbon Trust. https://www.carbontrust.com/what-we-do/market-transformation/maritime-decarbonisation

# 3. What the Finding Changes for Strategy, Claims, or Decisions

**1. Certification evaluation, not automatic adoption.**

*Analytical inference:* the Route to Net Zero Standard and the Supply Chain Standard are named, specific Carbon Trust certification products the workspace could evaluate for its own operations or recommend to clients; whether either is the right fit depends on which certification scheme the workspace's own client base already recognises, which the captured pool does not establish (Section 5).

**2. Maritime decarbonisation talking points, not a specific carrier or fuel recommendation.**

*Analytical inference:* the Carbon Trust's own alternative-shipping-fuels study (assessing five fuels for commercial readiness in the European context) is evidence a workspace can cite that structured, independent-organisation analysis of ocean-freight fuel alternatives exists; it does not itself establish which fuel is commercially ready today, since the study's findings themselves are not reproduced in the captured pool (Section 5).

**3. The Carbon Trust's own targets are a credibility reference, not the workspace's targets.**

FACT: "Reduce our Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 50% by 2030 from a 2018 base year Reduce our business travel emissions by 65% per FTE by 2030 from a 2018 base year." *Source: Carbon Trust Impact Report 2024. https://publications.carbontrust.com/

*Analytical inference:* these are the Carbon Trust's own internal decarbonisation targets (as an organisation), not a regulatory requirement placed on the workspace. They are useful as an illustration of what a credentialed advisory organisation sets for itself, not as a benchmark the workspace is obligated to meet.

# 4. Client Conversation Talking Points and Public Position

**What the workspace can credibly say:**

- "The Carbon Trust, a UK-incorporated, non-shareholder certification and advisory body that has supported over 2,796 organisations, operates both a Route to Net Zero Standard and a Supply Chain Standard, and cites the IMO's own finding that shipping represents almost 3% of global CO2 emissions in its maritime decarbonisation work."
- "The Carbon Trust is a founding partner of Blue Visby, an initiative aimed at reducing unnecessary fuel consumption in shipping through operational rather than technological change."

**Pitfalls to avoid:**

- Do not cite the 400-business Net Zero-barriers survey with specific statistics without having read the full published report; the captured page states the survey exists but does not reproduce its findings.
- *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a Carbon Trust certification (Route to Net Zero Standard or Supply Chain Standard) satisfies the substantiation requirements of the EU Green Claims Directive, or any equivalent green-claims regulation in a jurisdiction the workspace operates in, is a legal question this brief does not answer.
- Do not claim that Carbon Trust certification automatically satisfies any specific client's own procurement or sustainability framework; that is a client- and tender-specific question, not established by the captured pool.
- Do not present the Carbon Trust's certification schemes as UKAS-accredited; the Wikipedia source states they are not.

# 5. What the Finding Does Not Resolve

GAP: Legal Confirmation Required: whether a Carbon Trust certification satisfies the substantiation requirements of the EU Green Claims Directive, or an equivalent regime, is not established by the captured pool.

GAP: The fee structure, audit frequency, or contractual terms of Carbon Trust certification services are not available from primary sources.

GAP: Whether the Carbon Trust's certifications are accepted by any specific client's procurement or sustainability framework is client- and tender-specific and not established by this pool.

GAP: The specific philanthropic partners and programme designs under any Carbon Trust philanthropic-partnerships programme are not available from primary sources.

GAP: How the Carbon Trust's product-carbon-footprint methodology compares to ISO 14067 or the GHG Protocol Product Standard is not addressed in the captured pool.

GAP: The current status and findings of the Commercial Readiness of Alternative Shipping Fuels Study are not reproduced in the source blocks; only the study's existence and scope (five alternative shipping fuels, the European context) are stated.

FACT: "greenhouse gas emissions must fall by 43% by 2030. We are currently a long way from this goal. Climate targets have built an ambitious vision, but the focus now needs to be on action." *Source: Carbon Trust Impact Report 2024. https://publications.carbontrust.com/

FACT: "Engage with suppliers to ensure that by 2026 at least 56% of our suppliers by emissions are covered by a science-based target." *Source: Carbon Trust Impact Report 2024. https://publications.carbontrust.com/

FACT: "our Net Zero by 2050 target is in line with keeping global warming within 1.5C and has been validated by the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi)." *Source: Carbon Trust Impact Report 2024. https://publications.carbontrust.com/

*Operational implication:* the Carbon Trust's own admission that it is "currently a long way from" its science-aligned 43%-by-2030 reduction goal is a useful, honest data point for client conversations about how difficult even a well-resourced, credentialed advisory organisation finds its own science-aligned targets -- a caution against overpromising on the workspace's own trajectory.

- 2026: the Carbon Trust's own target is that at least 56% of its suppliers by emissions are covered by a science-based target.
- 2030: the Carbon Trust's own target is to reduce Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 50%, and business travel emissions by 65% per FTE, from a 2018 base year; the science-aligned goal it cites (43% economy-wide reduction by 2030) is one it states it is "currently a long way from."
- 2050: the Carbon Trust's own Net Zero target, validated by the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi).

# 1. What the Research Found

**MONITORING. Re-check window: the Barbados (28 May 2026) and Trinidad and Tobago (2 June 2026) national-assessment workshops, and UNCTAD's next annual Review of Maritime Transport.**

This item profiles the UNCTAD Transport Infrastructure and Services work programme and its Global Guidance on Port Resilience and Sustainable Freight Transport, drawing on UNCTAD's own topic page, its Review of Maritime Transport 2024, its Guidebook for Ports, the International Association of Ports and Harbors (IAPH), and the EU Maritime Safety Agency's own ETS extension page.

FACT: "The Transport Infrastructure and Services work programme supports developing countries in their effective integration into global and regional trade and value chains through efficient, reliable, cost-effective, environmentally friendly, climate-friendly, low-carbon, and socially inclusive freight transport systems." *Source: Transport Infrastructure and Services, UNCTAD. https://unctad.org/topic/transport-and-trade-logistics/infrastructure-and-services

FACT: "Sustainable freight transport Enable economically efficient, environmentally sound and socially inclusive freight transport and logistics Corridor performance Promote efficient transport corridors to support market and value chain integration Maritime transport Leverage shipping and ports to support economic growth and trade-led development" *Source: Transport Infrastructure and Services, UNCTAD. https://unctad.org/topic/transport-and-trade-logistics/infrastructure-and-services

FACT: "Cape of Good Hope arrivals surged 89%." *Source: Review of Maritime Transport 2024, UNCTAD. https://unctad.org/publication/review-maritime-transport-2024

FACT: "Ships have needed ship rerouting onto longer routes around the Cape of Good Hope, with ship transits running 70% down on the regular trend (Clarksons Research, 2025)." *Source: Review of Maritime Transport 2024, UNCTAD. https://unctad.org/publication/review-maritime-transport-2024

FACT: "By mid-2024, the Shanghai Containerized Freight Index (SCFI) had more than doubled from late 2023, driven by longer shipping distances, higher fuel consumption and rising insurance premiums." *Source: Review of Maritime Transport 2024, UNCTAD. https://unctad.org/publication/review-maritime-transport-2024

FACT: "For a 20,000-24,000 TEU vessel on the Far East-Europe route, CO2 emissions alone add $400,000 in costs under the European Union's Emissions Trading System." *Source: Review of Maritime Transport 2024, UNCTAD. https://unctad.org/publication/review-maritime-transport-2024

FACT: "From 1 January 2024, CO 2 emissions from ships of and above 5 000 gross tonnage, calling at or departing from ports in the European Economic Area (EEA)." *Source: ETS Extension to maritime, European Maritime Safety Agency (EMSA). https://www.emsa.europa.eu/reducing-emissions/extension-ets.html

FACT: "IAPH has developed into a global alliance of ports, representing today some 190 ports and 167 port-related businesses in 89 countries as of 6 December 2024." *Source: IAPH homepage / About IAPH. https://iaphworldports.org/

FACT: "The member ports together handle well over 60% of the world’s sea-borne trade and over 60% of the world container traffic." *Source: IAPH homepage / About IAPH. https://iaphworldports.org/

# 2. Why This Finding Matters Operationally and Commercially

FACT: "In this context, ports represent potential single points of failure in the maritime supply chain." *Source: Building Capacity to Manage Risks and Enhance Resilience: A Guidebook for Ports, UNCTAD. https://unctad.org/publication/building-capacity-manage-risks-and-enhance-resilience-guidebook-ports

*Operational implication:* UNCTAD's own guidebook frames ports as potential single points of failure in the maritime supply chain; for a freight-forwarding workspace, this is a direct argument for routing and carrier diversification at chokepoint-adjacent ports rather than concentrating volume through any one gateway.

FACT: "Although containerized shipments only represent about 16 percent of world maritime trade by volume, they account for more than 70 percent of its value." *Source: Review of Maritime Transport 2024, UNCTAD. https://unctad.org/publication/review-maritime-transport-2024

*Analytical inference:* because containerised cargo is disproportionately high-value relative to its physical volume share, a chokepoint disruption or a rerouting event (Section 1) has an outsized cost impact on containerised trade specifically -- directly relevant to the workspace's own high-value cargo verticals (fine art, luxury goods, film/TV, live events).

FACT: "Other relevant stakeholders include: (i) freight forwarders; (ii) customs authorities; (iii) carriers and shipping companies; (iv) shippers and cargo owners; and (v) inland carriers and inland logistics operators (e.g. dry ports, inland container depots, warehouses, logistics and distribution centres)." *Source: Building Capacity to Manage Risks and Enhance Resilience: A Guidebook for Ports, UNCTAD. https://unctad.org/publication/building-capacity-manage-risks-and-enhance-resilience-guidebook-ports

*Operational implication:* UNCTAD's own port-resilience guidebook names freight forwarders explicitly as a relevant stakeholder category in the port-resilience ecosystem it maps -- this is a direct institutional acknowledgement that the workspace's own role sits inside the resilience-planning conversation, not outside it.

FACT: "Effective adaptation action is particularly urgent as these assets are projected to be at high and increasing risk of coastal flooding, from as early as the 2030s (UNCTAD, 2019, 2020a)." *Source: Building Capacity to Manage Risks and Enhance Resilience: A Guidebook for Ports, UNCTAD. https://unctad.org/publication/building-capacity-manage-risks-and-enhance-resilience-guidebook-ports

FACT: "Extreme weather events which are projected to increase in frequency or severity under global warming (IPCC, 2023)." *Source: Building Capacity to Manage Risks and Enhance Resilience: A Guidebook for Ports, UNCTAD. https://unctad.org/publication/building-capacity-manage-risks-and-enhance-resilience-guidebook-ports

FACT: "ESLs of a magnitude so far expected to occur once a century, will occur much more often under climate change, significantly increasing the flood hazard for global ports, including some of the 100 largest container ports (figure 4)." *Source: Building Capacity to Manage Risks and Enhance Resilience: A Guidebook for Ports, UNCTAD. https://unctad.org/publication/building-capacity-manage-risks-and-enhance-resilience-guidebook-ports

*Operational implication:* the guidebook's own finding that a historically once-a-century extreme sea level event will recur much more often under climate change, affecting some of the 100 largest container ports, is a planning-horizon signal for any workspace with long-term facility, warehousing, or routing commitments at a major container port.

# 3. What the Finding Changes for Strategy, Claims, or Decisions

**1. EU ETS maritime cost pass-through is a live, quantified cost driver, not a future one.**

*Analytical inference:* the EU's Emissions Trading System extension to maritime has applied since 1 January 2024 (EMSA, Section 1), and UNCTAD's own worked example puts the CO2-emissions cost alone at $400,000 for a single large vessel on the Far East-Europe route. For workspaces booking ocean capacity on EU-calling routes, this is a quantified, current cost component to factor into rate expectations, not a future regulatory risk.

**2. Chokepoint rerouting (Suez/Cape of Good Hope) is the dominant near-term driver of transit-time and rate volatility on the affected lanes.**

*Analytical inference:* the Cape of Good Hope arrivals surge and the sustained 70% drop in the regular Suez transit trend (Section 1), combined with the more-than-doubled SCFI by mid-2024, together indicate that routing decisions on Asia-Europe lanes should be made with the expectation of continued elevated transit time and freight-rate volatility, not treated as a temporary disruption that will revert to the prior baseline on a known date.

**3. Port-resilience guidance is a citable, freight-forwarder-inclusive framework for client risk conversations.**

*Analytical inference:* because UNCTAD's own Guidebook for Ports explicitly names freight forwarders as a relevant stakeholder (Section 2), the workspace can cite this guidebook by name when discussing port-resilience planning with clients, rather than relying on generic climate-risk framing.

# 4. Client Conversation Talking Points and Public Position

**What the workspace can credibly say:**

- "UNCTAD's Review of Maritime Transport 2024 finds that Cape of Good Hope arrivals surged 89% as ships reroute away from the Suez Canal, with Suez transits running about 70% below the regular trend, and the Shanghai Containerized Freight Index more than doubled by mid-2024 as a result."
- "The EU's Emissions Trading System has applied to maritime CO2 emissions since 1 January 2024; UNCTAD's own worked example puts the added cost at roughly $400,000 for a single large vessel on the Far East-Europe route."
- "UNCTAD's own port-resilience guidebook names freight forwarders directly as a relevant stakeholder in port-resilience planning."

**Pitfalls to avoid:**

- Do not present the $400,000 EU ETS figure as applicable to every vessel or every route; it is UNCTAD's own worked example for a specific vessel-size band (20,000-24,000 TEU) on a specific route (Far East-Europe).
- *Legal Confirmation Required:* how the EU ETS maritime cost pass-through mechanism operates at the freight-forwarder level, as opposed to the carrier/vessel-operator level, is a legal and contractual question this brief does not resolve.

# 5. What the Finding Does Not Resolve

GAP: How the EU ETS cost pass-through mechanism operates at the freight-forwarder level is not resolved by the captured pool.

GAP: Whether a successor project with equivalent geographic scope and budget to the UNCTAD Sustainable Freight Transport capacity-building project (which ran 2014-2018 with a budget of $ 611,000) has been commissioned is not confirmed in the captured pool.

GAP: The Guidebook for Ports (UNCTAD/TCS/DTL/INF/2022/3) does not publish a formal update cycle or revision schedule in the captured pool.

GAP: Knowledge gaps persist, per UNCTAD's own guidebook, regarding individual coastal transport facilities' vulnerabilities and exposure, which the captured pool does not resolve.

FACT: "Duration 2014-2018 Budget $ 611,000" *Source: Building capacities of developing countries to shift towards sustainable freight transport, UNCTAD. https://unctad.org/project/building-capacities-developing-countries-shift-towards-sustainable-freight-transport

FACT: "Knowledge gaps persist, however, regarding individual coastal transport facilities’ vulnerabilities and exposure, hampering effective prevention and underlining the need for further research, guidance and capacity-building." *Source: Building Capacity to Manage Risks and Enhance Resilience: A Guidebook for Ports, UNCTAD. https://unctad.org/publication/building-capacity-manage-risks-and-enhance-resilience-guidebook-ports

FACT: "Improved monitoring systems for early detection of chokepoint disruptions and faster rerouting, as well as investment in early warning systems for ports." *Source: Transport Infrastructure and Services, UNCTAD. https://unctad.org/topic/transport-and-trade-logistics/infrastructure-and-services

FACT: "Strengthened international cooperation to stabilize trade routes, enhance resilience and minimize supply chain disruptions from geopolitical and climate-related risks." *Source: Transport Infrastructure and Services, UNCTAD. https://unctad.org/topic/transport-and-trade-logistics/infrastructure-and-services

FACT: "The guidebook presents a step-by-step approach to resilience building in the maritime supply chain. It sets out risk identification, assessment and management tools and techniques, and describes a resilience-building process for ports." *Source: Building Capacity to Manage Risks and Enhance Resilience: A Guidebook for Ports, UNCTAD. https://unctad.org/publication/building-capacity-manage-risks-and-enhance-resilience-guidebook-ports

FACT: "The guidebook is aimed at stakeholders across the maritime supply chain involved in building port resilience, and more specifically key actors and stakeholders participating in the port ecosystem while operating, managing or regulating port-related transport and logistics chains." *Source: Building Capacity to Manage Risks and Enhance Resilience: A Guidebook for Ports, UNCTAD. https://unctad.org/publication/building-capacity-manage-risks-and-enhance-resilience-guidebook-ports

FACT: "Building Capacity to Manage Risks and Enhance Resilience: A Guidebook for Ports (UNCTAD/TCS/DTL/INF/2022/3 ) 1 Aug 2022." *Source: Building Capacity to Manage Risks and Enhance Resilience: A Guidebook for Ports, UNCTAD. https://unctad.org/publication/building-capacity-manage-risks-and-enhance-resilience-guidebook-ports

FACT: "Review of Maritime Transport 2024 22 Oct 2024" *Source: Review of Maritime Transport 2024, UNCTAD. https://unctad.org/publication/review-maritime-transport-2024

FACT: "2 June 2026 Workshop to present and validate the Trinidad and Tobago’s national assessment: Focus on transport and logistics for sustainable and resilient food supply chains" *Source: Transport Infrastructure and Services, UNCTAD. https://unctad.org/topic/transport-and-trade-logistics/infrastructure-and-services

FACT: "28 May 2026 Workshop to present and validate the Barbados national assessment: Focus on transport and logistics for sustainable and resilient food supply chains" *Source: Transport Infrastructure and Services, UNCTAD. https://unctad.org/topic/transport-and-trade-logistics/infrastructure-and-services

FACT: "IAPH has consultative status and works on behalf of ports with additional United Nations bodies such as the UNCTAD (UN Conference on Trade and Development), UNEP (UN Environment Program) and the UN Global Compact." *Source: IAPH homepage / About IAPH. https://iaphworldports.org/

- 1 Aug 2022: UNCTAD published the Building Capacity to Manage Risks and Enhance Resilience: A Guidebook for Ports (UNCTAD/TCS/DTL/INF/2022/3).
- 1 January 2024: the EU's Emissions Trading System extended to maritime CO2 emissions for ships above 5,000 gross tonnage calling at or departing EEA ports.
- 22 Oct 2024: UNCTAD published the Review of Maritime Transport 2024.
- 6 December 2024: IAPH's stated membership figures (190 ports, 167 port-related businesses, 89 countries) are as of this date.
- 28 May 2026: workshop to present and validate the Barbados national assessment on sustainable and resilient food supply chains.
- 2 June 2026: workshop to present and validate the Trinidad and Tobago national assessment on sustainable and resilient food supply chains.

entries.body:
# 1. What the Research Found

**MONITORING. Re-check window: the next IRENA Collaborative Framework on Critical Materials meeting and the next annual IEA Global Critical Minerals Outlook.**

This item corroborates an IRENA press release and Collaborative Framework page against two IEA reports (EV Battery Supply Chain Sustainability; Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2024) and the Policy Commons catalogue entry for the underlying IRENA report.

FACT: "the growing demand for electric vehicle (EV) battery materials required by 2030 can be met by expanding sustainable supply chains and scaling-up the development and adoption of innovative technologies." *Source: IRENA press release, "Innovation and Sustainable Mining are Key to Meeting EV Demand for Critical Materials." https://www.irena.org/News/pressreleases/2024/Sep/Innovation-and-Sustainable-Mining-are-Key-to-Meeting-EV-Demand-for-Critical-Materials

FACT: "The report shows that meeting this target requires EV battery production to grow five-fold by 2030, necessitating a proportional rise in raw material supply to avoid supply-demand imbalances." *Source: IRENA press release. https://www.irena.org/News/pressreleases/2024/Sep/Innovation-and-Sustainable-Mining-are-Key-to-Meeting-EV-Demand-for-Critical-Materials

*Analytical inference:* this is IRENA's own stated conditional (production must grow to meet the target the report scopes), not a regulatory requirement placed on the workspace; it is read here as a market-demand signal, not a compliance obligation.

FACT: "Global EV sales are set to grow strongly, more than tripling by 2030 in the STEPS and APS to almost 45 million and 50 million vehicles, respectively, and increasing more than fivefold to 70 million in the NZE Scenario." *Source: IEA, Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2024, "Outlook for key minerals." https://www.iea.org/reports/global-critical-minerals-outlook-2024/outlook-for-key-minerals

FACT: "Battery demand is set to continue growing fast based on current policy settings, increasing four-and-a-half times by 2030 and more than seven times by 2035." *Source: IEA, EV Battery Supply Chain Sustainability. https://www.iea.org/reports/ev-battery-supply-chain-sustainability

FACT: "In the STEPS, demand doubles to 2030 with continued growth thereafter." *Source: IEA, Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2024. https://www.iea.org/reports/global-critical-minerals-outlook-2024/outlook-for-key-minerals

FACT: "Lithium presents another significant challenge, exhibiting a substantial anticipated gap with climate-driven needs, owing to the strong position of lithium-ion batteries in EVs and storage applications." *Source: IEA, Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2024. https://www.iea.org/reports/global-critical-minerals-outlook-2024/outlook-for-key-minerals

FACT: "Natural graphite production is expected to fall short of meeting the total graphite demand by 2030. Synthetic graphite and innovations in emerging anode technologies can bridge the supply-demand gap." *Source: IRENA press release. https://www.irena.org/News/pressreleases/2024/Sep/Innovation-and-Sustainable-Mining-are-Key-to-Meeting-EV-Demand-for-Critical-Materials

FACT: "recycling can reduce lithium and nickel demand by 25%, and cobalt demand by 40% in 2050, in a scenario that meets national climate targets." *Source: IEA, EV Battery Supply Chain Sustainability. https://www.iea.org/reports/ev-battery-supply-chain-sustainability

FACT: "cobalt and nickel no longer used in about half of the passenger EVs sold in 2023." *Source: IRENA press release. https://www.irena.org/News/pressreleases/2024/Sep/Innovation-and-Sustainable-Mining-are-Key-to-Meeting-EV-Demand-for-Critical-Materials

FACT: "Its criticality may decrease due to the rise of alternative technologies like LFP and LMFP." *Source: IRENA press release. https://www.irena.org/News/pressreleases/2024/Sep/Innovation-and-Sustainable-Mining-are-Key-to-Meeting-EV-Demand-for-Critical-Materials

FACT: "Demand is expected to remain high across all battery technology scenarios. Emerging technologies like sodium-ion, which do not rely on lithium, may enter the market later this decade, but their impact on reducing lithium demand will likely be more significant after 2030." *Source: IRENA press release. https://www.irena.org/News/pressreleases/2024/Sep/Innovation-and-Sustainable-Mining-are-Key-to-Meeting-EV-Demand-for-Critical-Materials

# 2. Why This Finding Matters Operationally and Commercially

FACT: "the geographical concentration of mining operations is set to remain high in most cases." *Source: IEA, Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2024. https://www.iea.org/reports/global-critical-minerals-outlook-2024/outlook-for-key-minerals

FACT: "the market value for refining is notably more concentrated, with China claiming nearly 50% of the market value in 2030." *Source: IEA, Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2024. https://www.iea.org/reports/global-critical-minerals-outlook-2024/outlook-for-key-minerals

*Operational implication:* both the geographical concentration of mining and China's near-50% share of energy-transition-mineral refining value by 2030 are direct supply-chain concentration risks for a workspace moving EV batteries or battery materials -- a disruption at a small number of mining or refining chokepoints has an outsized effect on this specific cargo category.

FACT: "Battery-related emissions play a notable role in electric vehicle (EV) life cycle emissions" *Source: IEA, EV Battery Supply Chain Sustainability. https://www.iea.org/reports/ev-battery-supply-chain-sustainability

FACT: "the emissions of a medium-size battery electric car are half the emissions of an equivalent internal combustion engine (ICE) car as a global average." *Source: IEA, EV Battery Supply Chain Sustainability. https://www.iea.org/reports/ev-battery-supply-chain-sustainability

*Analytical inference:* the IEA's global-average finding that a battery electric car's lifecycle emissions are half an equivalent ICE car's, combined with its own finding that battery-related emissions are a notable share of that total, together indicate that the battery-materials supply chain itself (mining, refining, transport of the materials the workspace may be moving) is where a meaningful share of the EV's own emissions footprint sits.

# 3. What the Finding Changes for Strategy, Claims, or Decisions

**1. Airfreight demand signal for qualification-phase and replenishment-tier battery-material shipments.**

*Analytical inference:* both IRENA and the IEA independently project EV battery production growing four-to-five times by 2030 (Section 1); for a workspace moving battery materials or components, this points to sustained upward pressure on both airfreight (for qualification-phase, time-critical, or emergency-replenishment shipments) and ocean freight (for bulk raw-material and cell shipments) volumes through 2030, not a one-off demand spike.

**2. Supply concentration risk should inform routing and contingency planning, not just capacity booking.**

*Analytical inference:* because mining concentration remains high and refining value is concentrating further toward China (Section 2), a workspace with recurring battery-material lanes should treat single-origin or single-transhipment-point dependency as a named operational risk, not an assumed constant.

**3. Substitution trends (cobalt/nickel, sodium-ion) change the material mix over time, not the freight volume trend.**

*Analytical inference:* IRENA's own finding that cobalt and nickel are already absent from about half of 2023 passenger EVs, and that sodium-ion batteries may gain share later this decade, signals that the SPECIFIC materials a workspace handles on this lane may shift even as the overall freight volume trend (Section 1) continues upward -- a reason to track material-mix trends per client, not only aggregate volume.

# 4. Client Conversation Talking Points and Public Position

**What the workspace can credibly say:**

- "Both IRENA and the IEA independently project that global EV battery production needs to grow four-to-five times by 2030 to meet climate-aligned demand, which is a structural, multi-year freight-volume signal for battery-material supply chains."
- "The IEA's own analysis finds that a medium-size battery electric car's lifecycle emissions are, on global average, half those of an equivalent internal combustion engine car, with battery-related emissions playing a notable role in that total."

**Pitfalls to avoid:**

- *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether and to what degree the EU Battery Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2023/1542) imposes due-diligence documentation obligations on a freight forwarder handling battery materials, as distinct from an importer of record, manufacturer, or battery producer, is not established by this brief and requires legal review.
- Do not present either report's demand projections as certainties; both IRENA and the IEA condition their figures on named policy scenarios (STEPS, APS, NZE for the IEA), and the IEA states explicitly that demand projections "are subject to large variations."

# 5. What the Finding Does Not Resolve

GAP: Whether and to what degree the EU Battery Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2023/1542) imposes due-diligence documentation obligations on a freight forwarder handling battery materials, as distinct from an importer of record, manufacturer, or battery producer, is not established by the captured pool.

GAP: The IEA's lifecycle-emissions analysis covers vehicle-level emissions, not freight-transport emissions for the materials in transit; neither report quantifies the freight-transport-specific emissions share.

GAP: The compliance obligations of a freight forwarder specifically (as distinct from other supply-chain actors named in Section 5's EU Battery Regulation GAP above) are not established by the captured pool.

GAP: Neither report provides a probability distribution for its central demand scenarios.

FACT: "demand projections are subject to large variations, influenced not only by broader policy considerations (reflected in our energy scenarios) but also by technology costs and innovations, as well as behavioural factors." *Source: IEA, Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2024. https://www.iea.org/reports/global-critical-minerals-outlook-2024/outlook-for-key-minerals

FACT: "To date, four meetings of the Collaborative Framework on Critical Materials for the Energy Transition (CFCM) have taken place. The latest CFCM meeting, held on October 24th, 2024." *Source: IRENA, Critical materials collaborative framework page. https://www.irena.org/How-we-work/Collaborative-frameworks/Critical-materials

FACT: "The Policy Commons catalogue entry records the underlying IRENA report at Pages 76 pages, catalogued 26 Sep 2024." *Source: Policy Commons catalogue entry for "Critical Materials for Electric Vehicle Batteries: An IRENA Analysis." https://policycommons.net/artifacts/16845709/critical-materials/17730542/

FACT: "Published 19 December 2024" *Source: IEA, EV Battery Supply Chain Sustainability. https://www.iea.org/reports/ev-battery-supply-chain-sustainability

- 24 Oct 2024: the fourth (most recent) meeting of IRENA's Collaborative Framework on Critical Materials for the Energy Transition (CFCM).
- 19 Dec 2024: the IEA's EV Battery Supply Chain Sustainability report was published.
- 26 Sep 2024: the Policy Commons catalogue entry date for the underlying IRENA report.

# 1. What the Research Found

**MONITORING. Re-check window: the trial's next reporting milestone and DP World's stated strategic-review outcome on permanently electrifying its route.**

FACT: "Called Project JOLT – standing for Joint Operator Logistics Trial – the programme is led by The Centre for Sustainable Road Freight (SRF) and involves partners including John Lewis Partnership, Volvo Trucks UK, and Flexible Power Systems, a software company specialising in fleet management optimisation software for electric vehicles." *Source: Electric HGV trial, University of Cambridge Department of Engineering. https://www.eng.cam.ac.uk/electric-hgv-trial

FACT: "SRF was founded to help industry and government minimise carbon emissions from the road freight sector and is a collaboration between Cambridge University, Heriot-Watt University in Edinburgh, the University of Westminster, and industry and government partners." *Source: Electric HGV trial, University of Cambridge Department of Engineering. https://www.eng.cam.ac.uk/electric-hgv-trial

FACT: "The objective is to develop the knowledge and models needed to de-risk electric freight operations and inform investment decisions." *Source: Electric HGV trial, University of Cambridge Department of Engineering. https://www.eng.cam.ac.uk/electric-hgv-trial

FACT: "It is driven by the Centre for Sustainable Road Freight and is made up of 15 fleet operators, four manufacturers, a charge point operator and three enablers." *Source: Electric HGV trial, University of Cambridge Department of Engineering. https://www.eng.cam.ac.uk/electric-hgv-trial

FACT: "Evyve, the charge point operator, is providing high powered charging infrastructure and energy solutions for the initiative and subsequent roll outs." *Source: Electric HGV trial, University of Cambridge Department of Engineering. https://www.eng.cam.ac.uk/electric-hgv-trial

FACT: "HGVs also account for 20% of CO 2 emissions from domestic transport." *Source: Electric HGV trial, University of Cambridge Department of Engineering. https://www.eng.cam.ac.uk/electric-hgv-trial

FACT: "98% of our food and agricultural products are carried by road, mostly on HGVs." *Source: Electric HGV trial, University of Cambridge Department of Engineering. https://www.eng.cam.ac.uk/electric-hgv-trial

FACT: "Freight is hugely important; it contributed £13.6 billion to the economy in 2022*." *Source: Electric HGV trial, University of Cambridge Department of Engineering. https://www.eng.cam.ac.uk/electric-hgv-trial

FACT: "DP World has successfully trialled three electric vehicles under the Project Jolt initiative, which it joined three months ago. The three electric trucks were the Scania G230E truck and the Mercedes e-Actros 300, which was upgraded to the e-Actros 600 in the final 3 weeks." *Source: "DP World hails success of Project Jolt electric truck trial," Motor Transport, 12 August 2025. https://motortransport.co.uk/freightcarbonzero/dp-world-hails-success-of-project-jolt-electric-truck-trial/26783.article

FACT: "The company said that, although the cost of the electric truck is still high, the likely cost of electricity will create a favourable total cost of ownership compared to diesel and then of course there are the huge environmental gains." *Source: Motor Transport, 12 August 2025. https://motortransport.co.uk/freightcarbonzero/dp-world-hails-success-of-project-jolt-electric-truck-trial/26783.article

FACT: "Following the trial, DP World and its customer have carried out a strategic review on the commercial opportunity to permanently electrify this route." *Source: Motor Transport, 12 August 2025. https://motortransport.co.uk/freightcarbonzero/dp-world-hails-success-of-project-jolt-electric-truck-trial/26783.article

# 2. Why This Finding Matters Operationally and Commercially

FACT: "The trial will pool operations and technical data from a fleet of rigid and articulated eHGVs being used across a wide range of 3PL, retailer and manufacturer use cases." *Source: Electric HGV trial, University of Cambridge Department of Engineering. https://www.eng.cam.ac.uk/electric-hgv-trial

*Operational implication:* because the trial pools data across 3PL, retailer and manufacturer use cases, a workspace operating UK road-freight subcontracts with any of these profiles could, in principle, be operating alongside a participating fleet already generating comparable operational data -- relevant context when a client asks whether eHGV total-cost-of-ownership data exists for their own use case.

FACT: "The trial is open to all HGV operators becoming involved by accessing a shared vehicle fleet supplied by OEMs or sharing data from their own vehicles." *Source: Electric HGV trial, University of Cambridge Department of Engineering. https://www.eng.cam.ac.uk/electric-hgv-trial

*Operational implication:* the trial's own stated openness to any HGV operator (via a shared OEM-supplied fleet or by sharing data from an operator's own vehicles) means the workspace's own road-freight subcontractors are, in principle, eligible to participate if not already doing so -- worth raising directly with a UK road subcontractor evaluating eHGV adoption.

FACT: "Specialists at Cambridge University and Heriot-Watt University will analyse and model data including vehicle and charger performance, operational efficiency, and costs across as many industry uses as possible." *Source: Electric HGV trial, University of Cambridge Department of Engineering. https://www.eng.cam.ac.uk/electric-hgv-trial

FACT: "High resolution operational data will be collected during each trial period and then analysed, anonymised, and shared with all partners as part of a managed collective learning process." *Source: Electric HGV trial, University of Cambridge Department of Engineering. https://www.eng.cam.ac.uk/electric-hgv-trial

FACT: "All shared data will be subject to the provisions of a Data Confidentiality Agreement which will be agreed between all partners before the work starts." *Source: Electric HGV trial, University of Cambridge Department of Engineering. https://www.eng.cam.ac.uk/electric-hgv-trial

# 3. What the Finding Changes for Strategy, Claims, or Decisions

**1. TCO signal for road subcontractor electrification conversations, sourced to a live commercial trial rather than a lab estimate.**

*Analytical inference:* DP World's own stated finding, that electricity cost creates a favourable total cost of ownership relative to diesel despite the electric truck's higher purchase cost, is a real-world commercial-operator statement, not a modelled projection; it strengthens the workspace's position when advising a client or road subcontractor evaluating eHGV adoption.

**2. A named-carrier permanent-electrification decision is pending, not yet made.**

FACT: "Following the trial, DP World and its customer have carried out a strategic review on the commercial opportunity to permanently electrify this route." *Source: Motor Transport, 12 August 2025. https://motortransport.co.uk/freightcarbonzero/dp-world-hails-success-of-project-jolt-electric-truck-trial/26783.article

*Operational implication:* DP World and its customer have only carried out a strategic review on permanently electrifying the trialled route; the workspace should not represent this route as already permanently electrified, and should monitor for the review's outcome (Section 5).

**3. Battery residual value remains an open research question, relevant to any road-fleet financing conversation.**

FACT: "Our research on battery performance is crucial to the ultimate findings on electrification and will help determine the residual value of electric trucks." *Source: Electric HGV trial, University of Cambridge Department of Engineering. https://www.eng.cam.ac.uk/electric-hgv-trial

*Analytical inference:* because the trial's own director frames battery residual value as still to be determined by this research, the workspace should treat eHGV residual-value assumptions in any client financing or leasing conversation as unresolved, not established.

# 4. Client Conversation Talking Points and Public Position

**What the workspace can credibly say:**

- "Project JOLT, a live UK research trial led by the Centre for Sustainable Road Freight (Cambridge and Heriot-Watt universities) with partners including John Lewis Partnership, Volvo Trucks UK, and DP World, is generating real-world operational data on electric HGVs across 3PL, retailer, and manufacturer use cases."
- "HGVs account for 20% of UK domestic transport CO2 emissions, and 98% of UK food and agricultural products move by road, mostly on HGVs -- context UNCTAD-scale figures the Cambridge trial page itself cites for why this research matters."
- "DP World's own trial experience found that, despite a higher electric-truck purchase price, expected electricity costs create a favourable total cost of ownership versus diesel."

**Pitfalls to avoid:**

- Do not state that DP World's trialled route is now permanently electrified; only a strategic review of the opportunity has been carried out, per the trial's own reporting.
- Do not cite a specific cost-per-kilometre or total-cost-of-ownership figure for eHGVs generally; these are not publicly available from the captured pool, which reports only DP World's own qualitative favourable-TCO statement for its own trial.
- *Legal Confirmation Required:* specific regulatory deadlines and penalty provisions for UK or EU HGV CO2 standards are not grounded in the captured source content and require separate legal/regulatory research.

# 5. What the Finding Does Not Resolve

GAP: Specific regulatory deadlines and penalty provisions for UK or EU HGV CO2 standards are not grounded in the captured source content.

GAP: Do not cite specific cost-per-kilometre or total-cost-of-ownership figures for eHGVs generally; these are not publicly available from the captured pool.

GAP: While DP World states that the likely cost of electricity will create a favourable TCO compared to diesel, the captured pool does not provide the underlying quantitative TCO calculation or timeframe.

FACT: "DP World hails success of Project Jolt electric truck trial By Carol Millett 12 August 2025" *Source: Motor Transport. https://motortransport.co.uk/freightcarbonzero/dp-world-hails-success-of-project-jolt-electric-truck-trial/26783.article

*Operational implication:* the workspace's next monitoring pass should check for the outcome of DP World's strategic review on permanent electrification of the trialled route, and for any published Project JOLT interim or final research findings beyond this initial trial-period reporting.

- 12 Aug 2025: Motor Transport reported DP World's successful trial of three electric vehicles (Scania G230E, Mercedes e-Actros 300 upgraded to e-Actros 600) under Project JOLT, joined approximately three months earlier.
